questions.q: For |ψ⟩ = 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩, what is the initial 8-amplitude teleportation state (q1 q2 q3, index = 4q1+2q2+q3) before any gates are applied?
questions.explain: Tensoring 0.6|0⟩+0.8|1⟩ with the Bell pair puts 0.6/√2≈0.4243 at indices 0 and 3, and 0.8/√2≈0.5657 at indices 4 and 7 -- the mirror image of the a=0.8,b=0.6 example from Lesson 20.

questions.q: In this lab's trace, if Alice measures '10', what raw (unnormalized) amplitudes does Bob's qubit hold, and what correction recovers |ψ⟩=(0.6,0.8)?
options: (0.3, -0.4), normalizing to (0.6, -0.8); applying Z flips the sign back to (0.6, 0.8)
(-0.4, 0.3), normalizing to (-0.8, 0.6); requiring X then Z
(0.3, 0.4), normalizing to (0.6, 0.8) directly; no correction needed
questions.explain: The '10' branch leaves Bob with a sign-flipped second amplitude, (0.6, -0.8); Z flips that sign back to (0.6, 0.8), which is the correct |ψ⟩, confirmed directly in node.

questions.q: What is the main point demonstrated by re-running the teleportation trace with a and b swapped (0.6, 0.8) instead of the original (0.8, 0.6)?
options: The Bell pair must be re-prepared differently for different a, b values
The same 00→I, 01→X, 10→Z, 11→XZ correction table works regardless of the specific a and b values -- it's a general property of the protocol, not an artifact of one example
Only the '00' branch still works when a and b are swapped
Swapping a and b breaks the protocol and no correction can recover |ψ⟩
questions.explain: All four correction branches converge to exactly the original |ψ⟩ in both the a=0.8,b=0.6 and a=0.6,b=0.8 cases, showing the correction table is a general fact about the circuit, not specific to one chosen state.

questions.q: If Alice encodes '10' with Z in superdense coding but Bob forgets to apply H before measuring (though he still applies CNOT correctly), what does Bob actually observe?
options: He measures all four outcomes with equal 25% probability
He reliably measures '01', the bit-flipped wrong answer
He measures '00' or '10' with 50% probability each, and never '01' or '11' -- the second bit always reads 0 and the first bit is a random coin flip
He reliably measures '10', exactly as if he had applied H
questions.explain: Computed directly: after CNOT alone (no H), the state is [0.7071, 0, -0.7071, 0], giving 50% probability each to |00⟩ and |10⟩ and exactly 0 to |01⟩ and |11⟩ -- the second bit is permanently stuck at 0 and the first bit becomes random.

questions.q: Why does skipping Bob's H gate in superdense coding break the protocol's guarantee, rather than just degrading it slightly?
options: Skipping H only matters for the message '00', not the other three

CNOT alone only un-spreads part of the entanglement; H is what converts the result into a basis where direct measurement reads out the message deterministically -- without it, one bit is lost entirely and the other becomes random
H is optional and only improves speed, not correctness
Skipping H has no real effect because CNOT alone always determines the full message
questions.explain: Both gates in the decode step are load-bearing: CNOT and H together are what make the readout deterministic (probability 1); removing either one collapses that guarantee rather than just reducing accuracy slightly.
